en: The Meaning Commentary on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*,
Recorded by the Great Master Tiantai Zhizhe: Now,
the Most Holy One bestowed his compassion, illuminating the capacities of beings and manifesting traces to guide those in the six realms and universally save those throughout the ten directions.
Rising and sinking according to circumstances, and becoming pure or defiled in accordance with conditions—this is the skillful means of gathering and guiding beings toward Bodhi.

Therefore, by the power of his ancient great vows, the Greatly Awakened Amitābha manifests a form in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, appearing within the site of enlightenment. Those of the three grades who aspire to be born there all enter the stage of certainty; their physical forms are most excellent, and their lifespans are inconceivable. Precious trees and celestial flowers are all able to expound the Dharma, while the pure breezes and flowing waters both proclaim sublime sounds; upon hearing these cries of suffering and emptiness, one realizes the patience of non-arising.

The Original Vow of the Holy Lord Śākyamuni is vast and profound; never abandoning his compassion, he transforms this defiled realm that is scorched by the five pains and oppressed by the eight sufferings. He extensively clarifies exhortations to reach all classes of beings, revealing the sublime method of rebirth through ten recitations. The fourfold assembly follows and practices according to these teachings; while the explanations vary in detail and differ according to time and place—proclaiming the three types of pure karma on Vulture Peak and expounding the protective mindfulness of the six directions at Śrāvastī—[the essence remains the same].
"Amitābha" is a Sanskrit term from India; in China it is translated as "Immeasurable Life. This is the auspicious name established for the supreme title of the Lord of Transformation.

As for "Sūtra," it is defined as "constant"; having issued from the mouths of the Sages, this specifically refers to what was spoken by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni concerning matters of the Western Quarter; therefore, it is called a "Sūtra."

This single teaching, though concise in its textual expression, is in fact rich in its elucidated meaning; it generally refers to the Western Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). First, regarding the explanation of its name:
the title is designated according to the person [who taught it], and by practicing in accordance with this teaching, one is reborn in that land.
The second clarifies the essence: through the contemplation and realization of the mind of the true suchness of dharmatā, one attains the fruits of permanence and bliss.
The third clarifies the fundamental purpose: through the karmic conditions of the pure land, the adornments of wondrous joy and transformational images welcome and gather in sentient beings.
The fourth power and function is the eradication of craving and views, such that the five stages of afflictions (*kleśa*) and their residual habits (*vāsanā*) are both exhausted.

The fifth aspect of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*) encompasses both the distinct and the universal; it brings forth the matured *tattva* (the "matured" stage) and the *amṛta* (the "ghee" stage), integrating them as the overall aspect of the teaching.
The text is divided into three sections: the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination. There is no separate introductory section;
rather, the six elements are contained within the general introduction.

First, regarding the phrase "Thus" (*evam*): it is a term of certainty. The Great Sage, observing the capacities of sentient beings, briefly expounded the profound and subtle for those with excessive anger, extensively revealed the secrets for those with excessive greed, and taught with moderation for those with excessive ignorance. His words do not issue in vain, but respond to things and adapt to conditions.

Regarding the phrase "I have heard": the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is immeasurable and boundless; that which I have been able to hear is like a mere drop of water, while that which I have not heard is comparable to the waters of the great ocean.
"At one time" means that when there is a stimulus, there is a response; at the very moment of awakening through such an opportunity, the assembly is transformed from the mundane into the sacred.

"Buddha" correctly designates the Master of Transformation: the Worthy One, the All-Knowing One, who possesses the four analytical knowledges, the six supernormal powers, the three types of clear knowledge, and the eight liberations; he expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet each being hears and understands it according to their own kind.

"Residing in Śrāvastī" refers to a place renowned for its fame and wealth, abounding in eminent and virtuous men, and rich in rare treasures; it is frequented by seekers of truth, merchants, and travelers from all nations, and is further known as a place where nothing exists that is not present.

Regarding "Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park": Jeta relinquished the trees to initiate the construction of the gates and courtyards, while Sudatta provided for the poor and covered the ground with gold coins to establish the vihāra together.

Regarding the phrase "together with a great community of bhikṣus," there are three meanings of "great": it is called "great" because it is revered by great beings such as celestial kings; it is called "many" because [the Buddha] has universally mastered both internal and external scriptures and teachings; and it is called "supreme" because it transcends the ninety-five [heterodox paths].
"Bhikṣu" means "one who dispels hunger. Regarding the three meanings pertaining to the causal stage:
one who begs for alms, one who terrifies Māra, and one who destroys evil. Regarding the three virtues of the resultant stage:
one worthy of offerings, one who has slain the thieves [of the afflictions], and one who does not arise [again].

The term "Saṃgha" refers to a community of four or more who perform formal acts (*karmavācanā*) in harmony; they maintain the separation between principle and practice to uphold and rectify the True Teaching. Regarding the phrase "together with twelve hundred and fifty people":

the group of the three Kāśyapas numbered one thousand, while Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana numbered two hundred and fifty. They constantly followed the Holy Honored One as a community of witnesses and believers. The Elder Śāriputra was the foremost in wisdom; he is translated as "Sparrow Son" (*Śāradvatīputra*).
Mahāmaudgalyāyana was renowned for his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*); this name is translated as "Reciter."
Mahākāśyapa is also called Pātra; this translates as "Turtle-clan" (Kauṇḍinya) or "Radiant Wave.
Mahākātyāyana was skilled at pure discourse; this translates as "Fan-cord.
Mahākauṣṭhila possessed unimpeded eloquence; this translates as "Great Thigh."
Lipatā is translated as the lunar mansion Śravaṇa, and is also called "Constant Sound.
Cūḷapanthaka, translated into the language of this land, means "Born by the Side of the Small Road.

Venerable Nanda is translated as "Delight"; Ānanda is translated as "Excellent Joy"; Rāhula is said here to mean "Obstructing Holder"; Gavāmpati is translated as "Cow’s Footprint"; Piṇḍola Bharadvāja is translated as "Running to Close the Door"; Kālodāyin is translated as "Great Coarse Black"; Kapphiṇa is translated as the lunar mansion Rohiṇī; Bakula is translated as "Good Appearance"; and Anuruddha is translated as "As One Wishes."

Mañjuśrī is translated here as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode); Ajita is translated as "Free from the Three Poisons"; Gandhahasti is translated as "Fragrant Mind"; and Sadāprarudita is a term from the dialect of this land.
The phrase "those such as these" concludes the assembly of bodhisattvas.
Śakra-devānām-indra is translated as "Lord of the Gods.

The phrase "and so forth" refers to the various hosts of devas; this collectively concludes the enumeration of those who heard the teaching, thereby completing the introductory section on the assembly.
The formal exposition consists of two parts:
first, clarifying the two fruits—the environment and the body—of that Buddha; second, exhorting beings to be reborn there.
The first part is further divided into two sections:
First the summary, then the explanation.
First the boundaries of the land are indicated, and subsequently the transforming master is clarified.

This sutra addresses Śāriputra by name; whereas other sutras all have various masters, this sutra is spoken ex cathedra without being questioned. Among the twelve divisions of the canon, it is not complete, lacking two types of verse, nor are the remaining divisions fully present.

Regarding those who are not bodhisattvas, the transformation is applied without fixed method, intended to cause ordinary beings and followers of the Lesser Vehicle to feel weary of this [state] and to aspire toward that [goal].
Within the exposition of the fruits of reliance (*niśraya-phala*), the preceding section clarifies the near and the far.

"The land named Sukhāvatī lies to the west, passing through a hundred thousand myriads of koṭis of Buddha-fields"—from the perspective of Master Xuánxiù, this is still an inferior grade; it is called "Supreme Bliss" (Sukhāvatī) only by comparison with the Saha world.

He has three names: "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī) is named in contrast to suffering; "Peaceful Nourishment" (An-yang) is derived from its function; and "Immeasurable Life" (Amitāyus) is named after the person and his land.

Next, he emerges with the title of the Perfect Fruit as Amitābha; although his life-span is actually finite, because other people cannot calculate its number, and since it is said that Avalokiteśvara is his successor (upapadya-bodhisattva), those on lower stages do not know it and thus speak of it as "immeasurable."
From the passage "Why is that land... onwards, there is an explanation of the previously clarified fruit of the support (*āśraya-phala*).
This consists of three parts:
first, the general; second, the specific; and third, the conclusion.
The initial general description follows the text as it stands.
From "the sevenfold rows of trees" onwards, there is a detailed explanation in four parts:
First, it clarifies the marvelous beauty of the jewel trees, ponds, and pavilions;
second, it clarifies how celestial flowers and celestial music serve as radiant adornments; third, it clarifies that these are proclaimed for the purpose of expounding the factors of the Path.
The four trees produce musical sounds.

These trees are sevenfold and composed entirely of the four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—and are surrounded by sevenfold nets and sevenfold rows of trees. When a gentle breeze stirs them, they emit harmonious sounds; upon hearing these sounds, one immediately enters the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
It is filled and overflowing with water possessing the eight virtues: light, clear, cool, soft, sweet, and odorless; it is perfectly suited when drunk and causes no ailment once consumed.
The bottom is strewn with golden sand, and the stairways on all four sides are composed of the four precious substances.
The lotuses in the pond are as large as chariot wheels, their radiant colors dazzling and their fragrance subtle, exquisite, and pure.
Above them are multi-storied pavilions, likewise adorned with the four precious substances.

Second, it clarifies that the music of the heavens is harmonious without being struck; from the strings emerge the sounds of immeasurable Dharma-transformations, which, when heard, inspire a heart of compassion, and upon hearing them, one immediately awakens to the Way.
Day and night, during the six periods, *mandārava* flowers rain down; these celestial blossoms are most exquisite and are named *mandārava*, their color unsurpassed and their fragrance fragrant.
Every morning at dawn, he would fill his robe-sleeve with flowers to offer to ten trillion Buddhas in other directions, returning to his own land by the time of the meal.
This "robe-sleeve" (yiji) was a vessel for holding flowers, shaped like a box with a single leg; he would hold it in his hands to present as an offering.
There are three kinds of multicolored birds—white cranes, peacocks, parrots, and mynas—as well as various waterfowl heard in this manner.
The kalaviṅka possesses a wondrous, pure, and lofty voice, which may be compared to the voice of the Buddha.
The *saṃjīvaka* has two heads on a single body; since their birth and death are simultaneous and equal, it is called "shared life.

These various birds, throughout the six periods of day and night, expound upon the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path. Their wondrous voices are harmonious and elegant, corresponding to the names and meanings of the dharmas within the *bodhipākṣika-dharmas*.
First are the five faculties (*pañcendriya*): faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Next, the five powers (*pañcabala*) are clarified; their names do not differ from those before, but as the faculties have developed power, they are designated by a different title.
The seven factors of enlightenment are mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, equanimity, concentration, and so forth.
The eightfold noble path consists of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
By skillfully cultivating the factors of enlightenment, one immediately attains the vision of the truths and reaches the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Do not say that these birds were born as a retribution for their misdeeds; rather, they are all manifestations created by that Buddha to cause the sound of the Dharma to flow forth.
The four directions are illuminated by sevenfold rows of trees and jeweled nets; their wondrous sounds are like hundreds of thousands of kinds of music playing simultaneously.
Spontaneously, all give rise to thoughts of mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and experience serene joy.
Next, the primary fruit is explained.
This section further consists of two parts:
first, the clarification of the teacher of transformation; second, the identification of the assembly of disciples.
The Master of Transformation has two further aspects:
first, the analysis of immeasurable radiance; second, the description of limitless lifespan.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If one wishes to attain immeasurable radiance and infinite lifespan, one should study Prajñā."
Regarding this assembly of followers, the Śrāvakas were previously distinguished and the Bodhisattvas are now clarified.
A question was raised earlier:
"It was previously stated that there are innumerable Śrāvakas; how can it later be said that all sentient beings born in that land are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive)?"
The commentary states:

In that land, even those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) are all non-retrogressive; the non-retrogression of the two vehicles refers to them becoming ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while the non-retrogression of bodhisattvas refers to their not falling back to the level of the Lesser Vehicle.
From the passage beginning with "Sentient beings who hear [this]" onwards is the second section, which exhorts others to seek rebirth there.
There are three parts:
first, the direct exhortation to be reborn there; second, the exhortation by means of scriptural citations; [and third, the exhortation through the example of others].
The threefold exhortation is further divided into two parts: first, the actual exhortation; second, the demonstration of the method for rebirth.
Regarding the first part, there are again two sections:
first, the actual exhortation; second, the explanation of the intent behind the exhortation.
"Śāriputra [attained rebirth] by means of slight merit," and so forth; next, the method is shown.
Question:

Previously it was said that one cannot [attain rebirth] by means of slight merit; why then does it later say that if the mind is not distracted for even one day or seven days, one will all attain birth?
Answer: It does not depend on the length of time in days, but specifically on the depth of one’s application of the mind.

If one can maintain single-mindedness without distraction for seven days, at the end of that person’s life, Amitābha Buddha will manifest transformation-buddhas to welcome them by the power of his past vows; with the mind undisturbed, they shall immediately attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
Why is this? Because if one applies oneself with earnest sincerity at the single thought-moment of death, one shall immediately attain rebirth.

"I see this benefit" is the explanation of this meaning: one should make vows and practice with a single mind; with vows adorning the practice and practice supporting the vows, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
The passage beginning with "As I do now" serves as a citation to provide scriptural evidence and exhortation.

It is not that I alone praise that Buddha; rather, it is to truly exhort all beings to be reborn there. All Buddhas of the six directions likewise exhort, inspire, proclaim, and praise those who will be reborn in that land from within their respective realms, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
If men or women hear the name of this sutra, they shall all be protected and remembered by all Buddhas, and all shall attain the non-retrogressive mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
Therefore, you should believe my words and the teachings of the Buddhas; you should make a vow to be born there, and all shall attain non-retrogression upon being reborn in that land.

Those Buddhas also praised Śākyamuni for performing a difficult feat: that within the defiled and evil realm of the five turbidities in Sahā, he has preached the Dharma that is difficult to believe for the sake of all sentient beings, and shall thereby attain Bodhi.

This defiled land is characterized by deep obstructions and heavy impurities of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). Greed and anger constitute the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*); the five views constitute the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). With these two as the basis, one grasps at them as causes, thereby obtaining a continuous life-force. Based upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one provisionally designates a "sentient being. The passage of time through these four [turbidities] is called the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

In defiled lands, suffering is abundant and their turbidity is extremely heavy; by dwelling together in a pure land, that turbidity becomes light. Because they accord with other regions, the name [of "defilement"] exists there, yet being free from such oppression and affliction, it is called "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī).
The section beginning with "After the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra" constitutes the section on circulation (*pravartana*).
Once the preaching of the sutra was completed, the fourfold assembly, devas, humans, asuras, and other such classes rejoiced, believed, and accepted it.

A Holy Sovereign is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower; today we rejoice at having seen him. The True Dharma is difficult to hear; now we hear it. That which was not previously realized has now been realized. Possessing these three joys, we are filled with delight; receiving this within our hearts, our exultation is immeasurable.
*Annotated Record of the Meaning of the Amitābha Sūtra*, one fascicle.
